questions.question: What is an Amazon Machine Image (AMI)?

options.text: A virtual hard disk attached to an EC2 instance
A template containing OS, software, and configuration used to launch EC2 instances
A snapshot of an EBS volume
A network interface for EC2 instances

explanation.correct: An AMI is a template that contains everything needed to launch an EC2 instance — the operating system, application software, and configuration settings.
explanation.why: A is an EBS volume, C is an EBS snapshot (a component that backs the AMI), D is an ENI.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component contained in an AMI?

options.text: Operating System
Application software
VPC routing tables
EBS snapshots

explanation.correct: AMIs contain OS, software, configuration, and EBS snapshots. VPC routing tables are part of the VPC configuration, not part of an AMI.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all components of an AMI. Routing tables belong to the network layer (VPC), not to the server image.

questions.question: When you launch an EC2 instance, selecting an AMI is:

options.text: Optional — you can skip it
Required — every instance must be launched from an AMI
Only required for Windows instances
Only required for instances with EBS storage

explanation.correct: Selecting an AMI is a required parameter every time you launch an EC2 instance. The AMI defines what the instance will contain.
explanation.why: There is no such thing as an EC2 instance launched without an AMI.

questions.question: Which AMI source contains clean, AWS-maintained operating systems like Amazon Linux 2023 and Ubuntu 22.04?

options.text: My AMIs
AWS Marketplace
Quick Start AMIs
Community AMIs

explanation.correct: Quick Start AMIs are provided and maintained directly by AWS. They contain clean OS installations with the latest security patches.
explanation.why: My AMIs are user-created. AWS Marketplace AMIs come from third-party vendors. Community AMIs are shared by the public.

questions.question: What is a Custom AMI (My AMI)?

options.text: An AMI provided by AWS with a custom operating system
An AMI you create from your own EC2 instance, capturing its software and configuration
An AMI purchased from the AWS Marketplace
An AMI that is shared publicly with all AWS users

explanation.correct: A custom AMI (shown as 'My AMIs' in the console) is one you create from a running EC2 instance. It captures everything installed on that instance.
explanation.why: AWS provides its own AMIs (Quick Start). Marketplace AMIs are third-party. Publicly shared AMIs are Community AMIs.

questions.question: What is an EBS Snapshot?

options.text: A backup of an AMI template
A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume
A copy of an EC2 instance's metadata
A saved network configuration

explanation.correct: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume — it captures the actual contents of the disk at the moment the snapshot is taken.
explanation.why: Snapshots back AMIs, but they are specifically backups of EBS volumes (hard disks), not AMI templates or metadata.

questions.question: When you create a Custom AMI from an EC2 instance, what does AWS automatically create in the background?

options.text: A new EC2 instance
A new VPC
An EBS Snapshot of the root volume
An Elastic IP address

explanation.correct: When you create a custom AMI, AWS automatically takes an EBS snapshot of the root volume (and any other attached volumes) to store the actual disk data that backs the AMI.
explanation.why: The AMI itself is just a reference/template — the actual data is stored in the EBS snapshot that AWS creates automatically.

questions.question: In which section of the EC2 console can you see all the AMIs you have created?

options.text: EC2 → Instances
EC2 → Volumes
EC2 → AMIs
EC2 → Snapshots

explanation.correct: Your custom AMIs are listed under EC2 → AMIs in the left sidebar of the EC2 console.
explanation.why: Instances shows running/stopped servers, Volumes shows EBS disks, Snapshots shows disk backups — AMIs has the image templates.

questions.question: What status must an AMI show before you can use it to launch instances?

options.text: pending
available
active
ready

explanation.correct: An AMI must have a status of 'available' before it can be used to launch EC2 instances. The status starts as 'pending' while the AMI is being created.
explanation.why: 'pending' means the AMI is still being created. Only 'available' means it is ready to use.

questions.question: What is the path in the AWS Console to create a Custom AMI from a running instance?

options.text: EC2 → Instances → Right-click → Create Snapshot
EC2 → Instances → Actions → Image and Templates → Create Image
EC2 → AMIs → Create AMI
EC2 → Volumes → Actions → Create Image

explanation.correct: To create a custom AMI, select the instance, then go to Actions → Image and Templates → Create Image.
explanation.why: You start from the instance you want to capture. There is no direct 'Create AMI' button on the AMIs page — you initiate it from the instance.

questions.question: An AMI created in the Mumbai (ap-south-1) region — which of the following is true?

options.text: It is automatically available in all AWS regions
It is only available in the Mumbai region unless explicitly copied
It is available in all regions within the Asia Pacific geography
It must be recreated from scratch in each region

explanation.correct: AMIs are region-specific. An AMI created in Mumbai is only available there. To use it in another region (e.g., North Virginia), you must explicitly copy it using Actions → Copy AMI.
explanation.why: AWS does not automatically replicate AMIs across regions. You control where your AMIs exist.

questions.question: What is the correct action to copy an AMI from Mumbai to North Virginia?

options.text: EC2 → Instances → Migrate
EC2 → AMIs → Actions → Copy AMI → select destination region
EC2 → Snapshots → Actions → Copy to Region
EC2 → AMIs → Actions → Move AMI

explanation.correct: To copy an AMI to another region: go to EC2 → AMIs, select your AMI, then Actions → Copy AMI, and choose the destination region (e.g., us-east-1 for North Virginia).
explanation.why: There is no 'Move AMI' option (moving implies deletion from source). Snapshots have their own copy option but that is not the same as copying an AMI. You copy the AMI, not the instance.

questions.question: After copying an AMI to North Virginia, where do you go in the console to find it?

options.text: Stay in Mumbai region → EC2 → AMIs
Switch console to North Virginia region → EC2 → AMIs
Global Services → AMIs
It appears automatically in your EC2 Dashboard in all regions

explanation.correct: After copying an AMI to another region, you must switch your AWS Console to that region (North Virginia / us-east-1) and then navigate to EC2 → AMIs to see the copied AMI.
explanation.why: AWS console is region-scoped. Resources in one region are not visible when you have another region selected.

questions.question: You create a custom AMI from an 8 GB EBS volume. The snapshot created is only 1.6 GB. Why?

options.text: The AMI feature compresses data by default
EBS snapshots only capture the used portion of the volume, not the full allocated size
The snapshot is always 20% of the volume size
AWS only backs up the OS, not your data

explanation.correct: EBS snapshots capture only the data that is actually written to the volume — not the entire allocated size. An 8 GB volume with only 1.6 GB of data will produce a 1.6 GB snapshot.
explanation.why: This is not compression — it is incremental, used-block capture. Subsequent snapshots are incremental too (only changed blocks).

questions.question: What happens when you deregister an AMI?

options.text: The AMI and its EBS snapshot are both permanently deleted
The AMI template is removed, but the underlying EBS snapshot still exists and must be deleted separately
The AMI is moved to a deleted state but can be recovered within 30 days
All EC2 instances launched from that AMI are immediately terminated

explanation.correct: Deregistering an AMI only removes the AMI template (the reference). The underlying EBS snapshot that stores the actual data continues to exist and must be manually deleted to avoid ongoing storage charges.
explanation.why: This is a common mistake — students assume deregistering cleans up everything. You must separately go to Snapshots and delete the snapshot.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid reason to use a Custom AMI instead of a Quick Start AMI?

options.text: To get the latest AWS security patches
To launch instances with a pre-configured software stack without manual setup
To reduce EC2 compute costs
To run instances without specifying a key pair

explanation.correct: Custom AMIs let you capture a fully configured server state so that new instances launched from it already have all your software installed and configured — saving setup time at every launch.
explanation.why: Quick Start AMIs have latest patches (not custom ones). AMI choice does not affect compute cost or key pair requirements.

questions.question: A company maintains a 'golden AMI'. What does this mean?

options.text: An AMI provided by AWS for premium customers
A standardized, pre-approved AMI that ensures consistent configuration across all environments
An AMI with the most RAM and CPU resources
An AMI that is automatically updated by AWS

explanation.correct: A golden AMI is a standardized base image created and approved by an organization's team, containing all required software, security hardening, and configurations — ensuring consistency across dev, test, and production.
explanation.why: This is an organizational practice, not an AWS feature. 'Golden' refers to quality/standardization, not premium AWS status.

questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST use case for copying an AMI to another region?

options.text: To reduce EC2 instance costs in the source region
To enable multi-region deployment and serve users closer to their geography
To increase the storage capacity of the original AMI
To automatically back up running EC2 instances

explanation.correct: Copying an AMI to another region enables you to launch identical servers there — supporting multi-region architectures that serve users with lower latency by placing servers closer to them.
explanation.why: Copying does not reduce costs, increase storage, or back up running instances. It enables geographic distribution of your server blueprint.

questions.question: What is the correct order to completely remove an AMI and free all storage?

options.text: Delete snapshot → Deregister AMI
Deregister AMI → Delete the associated EBS snapshot
Terminate instances → Deregister AMI (snapshot is auto-deleted)
Delete AMI from the Snapshots page

explanation.correct: The correct order is: first Deregister the AMI (EC2 → AMIs → Actions → Deregister AMI), then separately delete the EBS snapshot (EC2 → Snapshots → Delete Snapshot).
explanation.why: You cannot delete a snapshot while an AMI is still registered to it — AWS will prevent it. Deregister first, then clean up the snapshot.

questions.question: In the session, the trainer launched a new server from a Custom AMI and found Apache already running. What does this confirm?

options.text: AWS automatically installs Apache on all EC2 instances
The AMI successfully captured the software configuration of the original instance
Apache was installed by the user during the launch wizard
The security group allowed Apache traffic automatically

explanation.correct: The fact that Apache was already running on the new instance (without any manual setup) confirms the custom AMI captured the software configuration of the original server.
explanation.why: AWS does not auto-install Apache. No software installation happens in the launch wizard. Security groups control access but do not install software.

questions.question: You need to deploy an application to 50 EC2 instances, all with the same configuration. Without AMIs, what would you need to do?

options.text: Use CloudFormation to auto-configure — AMIs are not needed
Manually set up each of the 50 instances individually
Use S3 to copy configuration files at launch
AMIs are always required, so this scenario is impossible without them

explanation.correct: Without a custom AMI, you would need to manually configure each of the 50 instances individually — installing software, setting up configs, etc. This is why custom AMIs are critical for scalable deployments.
explanation.why: While CloudFormation and user data scripts can automate some setup, the core point here is that without pre-baked AMIs, every instance starts from a blank OS and needs manual or scripted setup.

questions.question: An AMI created from an instance in us-east-1 has AMI ID ami-0abc123. If you copy this AMI to eu-west-1, what will the AMI ID be in eu-west-1?

options.text: ami-0abc123 (same ID in both regions)
A different, newly assigned AMI ID unique to eu-west-1
The original AMI ID with a region prefix: eu-west-1-ami-0abc123
AMIs do not have IDs — they are identified by name only

explanation.correct: When an AMI is copied to a new region, it is assigned a brand new, unique AMI ID in that region. The same AMI content will have different IDs in different regions.
explanation.why: AMI IDs are regional and globally unique within a region. AWS assigns a new ID in the destination region when you copy.

questions.question: What is the relationship between EBS Volume, EBS Snapshot, and AMI?

options.text: Volume → Snapshot (backup of volume) → AMI (references snapshot + launch config)
AMI → Volume → Snapshot
Snapshot → AMI → Volume
All three are the same thing with different names

explanation.correct: The correct relationship: EBS Volume is the live disk attached to a running instance. EBS Snapshot is a point-in-time backup of that volume. AMI references the snapshot and adds launch configuration metadata to form a complete server blueprint.
explanation.why: Understanding this chain is essential — the Volume is live storage, the Snapshot is the backup, the AMI wraps the snapshot with instance configuration to become launchable.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure all their EC2 instances always use the same hardened, patched OS. They update it monthly. Which approach is most scalable?

options.text: Manually update each running instance every month
Create a new 'golden AMI' each month and replace instances by launching from the new AMI
Use AWS Config to push patches to all instances automatically
Create one master instance and clone its hard drive manually

explanation.correct: The golden AMI pattern solves this: build a new patched AMI each month, then replace existing instances by launching fresh ones from the new AMI. This ensures all new capacity is always on the latest approved baseline.
explanation.why: Manual patching of running instances at scale is error-prone. AWS Config can help track compliance but is not the mechanism for distributing a hardened baseline. The golden AMI pattern is the industry standard.

questions.question: You have a t3.large EC2 instance with a custom AMI. You want to launch smaller t3.micro test instances from the same AMI. Is this possible?

options.text: No — AMIs are tied to the instance type they were created from
Yes — AMIs are independent of instance type; you can choose any compatible instance type at launch
Yes — but only if both instance types are in the same family (t3)
No — you need to create a separate AMI for each instance type

explanation.correct: AMIs are not tied to instance types. You can launch any compatible instance type from an AMI. An AMI created from a t3.large can launch t3.micro, m5.xlarge, or any other instance type that supports the same architecture (e.g., x86_64).
explanation.why: Instance type defines compute resources. AMI defines the software. They are independent selections in the launch wizard.

questions.question: In a disaster recovery scenario, what is the recommended practice regarding AMIs?

options.text: Keep one AMI per availability zone in the same region
Regularly create AMIs of production servers AND copy them to at least one other region
AMIs are not useful for disaster recovery — use RDS Multi-AZ instead
Take AMI backups only when making application changes

explanation.correct: Best practice for DR with AMIs is to regularly create AMIs of your production servers AND copy them to a different region. This ensures you can rebuild your environment even if the primary region has an outage.
explanation.why: Same-region AMIs cannot help if the entire region goes down. Cross-region AMI copies provide true geographic redundancy for disaster recovery.

questions.question: Which virtualization type do modern EC2 instances use when launched from current AMIs?

options.text: PV (Paravirtual)
HVM (Hardware Virtual Machine)
Full virtualization (FV)
Container-based (Docker)

explanation.correct: Modern EC2 instances and AMIs use HVM (Hardware Virtual Machine) virtualization. HVM provides better performance and supports all instance types. PV (Paravirtual) is a legacy option no longer used for new instances.
explanation.why: PV was the original EC2 virtualization type but is now legacy. HVM replaced it for performance and hardware compatibility reasons.

questions.question: What is charged when you store an AMI in AWS?

options.text: A flat monthly fee per AMI regardless of size
No charge — AMIs are free to store
Storage cost for the underlying EBS snapshots that back the AMI
Hourly charge based on the instance type the AMI was created from

explanation.correct: There is no charge for registering or storing an AMI registration itself. However, you are charged for the EBS snapshot storage that backs the AMI — approximately $0.05 per GB per month in most regions.
explanation.why: The AMI is just a reference/template. The actual data is in EBS snapshots, and snapshot storage is billed.

questions.question: A student copies an AMI from Mumbai to N. Virginia. They then deregister the AMI in N. Virginia. What happens to the original AMI in Mumbai?

options.text: It is also deregistered automatically
It is not affected — deregistering in one region only affects that region's copy
It is moved back to Mumbai since Virginia's copy was deleted
AWS prevents deregistration if the same AMI exists in another region

explanation.correct: AMI copies in different regions are completely independent resources. Deregistering an AMI in N. Virginia has no effect on the original AMI in Mumbai — they are separate copies.
explanation.why: Each Copy AMI operation creates a fully independent new AMI in the destination region. Actions on one do not affect the other.

questions.question: Which AWS service for DNS routing was mentioned as an upcoming topic in the session?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
Amazon Route 53
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon API Gateway

explanation.correct: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. The trainer mentioned it will be covered in the next session — it allows you to map domain names (like www.mywebsite.com) to your EC2 server's IP address.
explanation.why: CloudFront is a CDN. Direct Connect is a dedicated network link. API Gateway is for REST/HTTP APIs. Route 53 is the DNS service.
